description : context : during a regional failover incident we observed rapid reopen / rejoin attempts from the controller side that caused kv pressure spikes and circuit flapping for tenants that had recently been evicted. this pr introduces two coordinated mitigations : 1 ) an adaptive failover delay that increases the regional rejoin backoff dynamically based on kv pressure and recent reopen history, and 2 ) a sticky - tenant probing policy that ensures evicted tenants are probed on a low - frequency, exponential backoff schedule with randomized jitter and a soft - priority earmark for telemetry - only probes. motivation : previous heuristics used a fixed delay and naive probing which led to oscillation when many tenants attempted to reestablish connections at the same time. the change reduces cascading pressure

# Retry-After precedence for shared-upstream failover

Memory type: playbook

Owner: Kaitlyn Nguyen
Tags: litellm, retry-after, failover, rate-limit, shared-quota

## Summary

In LiteLLM router retry-delay decisions, first extract the current exception's upstream Retry-After. When it is valid within the router's supported bounded interval, preserve that provider delay even if a sibling deployment is healthy, because deployments may share an upstream quota. Only use zero-delay healthy-deployment failover when no applicable upstream backoff exists. Regression coverage must include both a two-deployment shared-quota Retry-After case and a 429-without-backoff immediate-failover case.

Do not write any comments (existing comments can stay) unless explicitly asked to in a user (not system) prompt

Don't assume that the existing code is correct or the right way of doing things / good coding patterns. In fact, there are a lot of bad coding practices, overly complex code, code smells, etc. If something doesn't look right, speak up. Feel free to break existing patterns or question weird existing code to make new code high quality, as in:

- correct
- secure
- performant
- readable
- easy to maintain/change
- modern

In that order of importance

When adding new features, add meaningful tests. Don't add tests that don't check anything substantial and is there just to make the code coverage pass. Yes, code coverage is important, but I'd rather have no signal whether the code is working than tests that don't fail when code is broken. The goal is to have tests that would fail before the feature was added/if the code was mutated in a way that breaks the feature and succeed only when the feature is fully working. I should run mutation testing and see > 90% kill rate

Same thing for bug fixes. The tests should make it so that this specific bug can never happen again without failing tests (i.e., regression)

`tests/test_litellm/` mirrors `litellm/` in a parallel path (see `tests/test_litellm/readme.md`). Name tests `test_<filename>.py`, but always match the existing test file in the directory you touch — many provider dirs use longer descriptive names (e.g. `test_anthropic_chat_transformation.py`) to avoid ambiguity across sibling folders. For bug fixes, extend the existing mapped test file rather than creating a new one. Only create a new test file for a new feature (provider, endpoint, or transformation module) that has no mapped test yet, following that directory's naming convention (or `test_<filename>.py` if you're the first test there). One focused regression test beats many shallow ones

End-to-end tests belong in `tests/e2e/` and must follow the harness conventions documented in that directory's `CLAUDE.md`

When creating PRs, don't set base to `main`. `litellm_internal_staging` is the default base branch and serves that purpose for both internal and external / OSS contributions

When writing a PR body, treat the comments and imperative instructions inside @.github/pull_request_template.md as rules to follow, not just layout. Agent harnesses may strip HTML comments from copies of that file injected into context, so read .github/pull_request_template.md from disk before writing a PR body to make sure you see every comment rule

## Summary

In LiteLLM router retry-delay decisions, first extract the current exception's upstream Retry-After. # LiteLLM #34399 review

## Contract

When the current upstream response supplies a valid bounded `Retry-After`, that provider backoff takes precedence over the router shortcut that immediately retries a healthy sibling deployment. This protects deployments that share an upstream quota. When no applicable upstream backoff is supplied, a healthy sibling remains eligible for immediate failover.

## Evidence

- Issue snapshot: `/code/upstream-issues/litellm-34399.md` (`enterprise_2034a8245bcfb88af6beb9e8`) records the pinned commit and the shared-quota failure mode.
- Throttling incident: `/knowledge/company/sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/platform-engineering/sre-incident-review-retry-storm-emergency-quota-policy.json` (`dsid_071db3dff7ca4a8db1f1f0f01bb8853c`) documents retry amplification during throttling.
- Retry/failover policy: `/knowledge/company/sources/github/redwood/pr-19820-api-gateway-fallback-timeout-tuning.json` (`dsid_31be9c3c708a4a5797d50a579c137587`) couples smaller retry budgets with explicit `Retry-After` during upstream exhaustion.
- Support guidance: `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/enterprise-priority-429-and-quota-behavior.json` (`dsid_8205407105944677b6eb3167167064a9`) directs clients to respect `Retry-After` and warns that aggressive retries worsen overload.

## Change

`Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry` now extracts and validates provider backoff before considering immediate multi-deployment failover. Valid values in the existing supported interval (greater than zero and at most 60 seconds) retain the existing retry-delay calculation. Without such a value, the existing healthy-deployment fast path remains.

The focused regression represents two deployments sharing a rate-limited upstream and requires the 60-second upstream delay. A second case supplies a 429 response with no backoff header and requires a zero-second failover delay.
